summary: Asks the IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority to allocate an Information Element number to the IETF in the IEEE 802.15.4 registry. It also describes how that element is formatted so that subtypes can be defined under it.

plainLanguage.summary: Low-power radio frames can carry extra pieces of information called information elements. This document asks for one such element to be set aside for IETF protocols, explains how an IETF element is laid out, and sets up the registry that decides which protocol uses which number inside it.

subtitle: How IETF protocols carry their own data in IEEE 802.15.4 low-power radio frames.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 lets other standards add their own data to radio frames through Information Elements, but each standards body has to be given its own element number before it can do so.
tldr.mechanism: The document asks the IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority for one element number for the IETF, and describes how that element carries a subtype number and the subtype's content.
tldr.outcome: The IEEE 802.15 Working Group allocated element number 5 for IETF use, and the document creates the IANA registry that assigns the subtype numbers inside it.

today: RFC 8137 is an Informational document published in May 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The IEEE 802.15 Working Group has already allocated element number 5 for IETF use, and the document creates the registry of subtype numbers that IANA maintains.

sections.title: Why the IETF Needs Its Own Element
sections.content:
IEEE Std 802.15.4 enables very low-cost and low-power communications. The standard defines numerous optional Physical Layers operating in many different frequency bands with a simple and effective Medium Access Control layer, and it defines Information Elements that can be used to extend 802.15.4 in an interoperable manner. An IE provides a flexible, extensible and easily implementable method of encapsulating information. The general format of an IE consists of an identification field, a length field and a content field. Multiple IEs may be concatenated, and elements with unknown ID values in a list can be skipped since their length is known, so IEs give a flexible container that lets new definitions be added in future versions of the standard in a backwards-compatible manner.

There are two different IE types. A Header IE is part of the MAC header; it is never encrypted, but it may be authenticated, and most of the Header IE processing is done by the MAC. A Payload IE is part of the MAC payload and may be encrypted and authenticated.

IETF protocols need to insert information into 802.15.4 frames, and the standard enables that by including one or more payload IEs in the frame. For this purpose the IETF requests a dedicated Payload IE from the IEEE 802.15 Assigned Numbers Authority, which manages the registry of Information Elements.

The 802.15 operations manual describes how a Standards Development Organization may request the allocation of one IE. To make the request the organization has to provide the reason for the request, a description of the protocol format that shows an appropriate subtype capability, and an agreement that only one IE number will be allocated for its use. This document provides the information needed for that request.
sections.plainLanguage: 802.15.4 frames can hold extra fields, and each organisation that wants one needs a number of its own. The document asks for a single number for the IETF, along with the promise that no second number will be needed, which is what the IEEE's own process requires.

sections.title: The IETF Information Element Format
sections.content:
The maximum length of the Payload IE content is 2047 octets, and the 802.15.4 frame contains a list of payload IEs. A single frame can have multiple payload IEs, terminated with the payload IE terminator, which may then be followed by the payload.

Since the 802.15.4 standard defines the list of payload IEs along with their structures, there is no need for this document to specify the internal nesting structure of the IETF IE. The Payload IE format of the 802.15.4 standard contains the Length field, so the length of the subtype content can be calculated from the Payload IE Length field of the IETF IE.

The format of the IETF IE starts with a Subtype ID octet and is followed by the subtype content. The Subtype ID is the IANA-allocated number specifying the subtype of the IETF IE; value 0 is reserved for future extensibility, that is, in case a longer subtype ID field is needed. The subtype content is the actual content of the Information Element, and its length can be calculated from the Length field of the IETF IE. One 802.15.4 frame MAY contain multiple IETF IEs with the same or different subtypes.
sections.plainLanguage: The element holds a number that says which protocol the content belongs to, followed by that protocol's own bytes. The length of the content comes from the length field the 802.15.4 format already provides, so nothing extra has to be defined. A frame can carry several such elements.

sections.title: Which Working Groups Benefit
sections.content:
There are several IETF working groups, such as 6TiSCH, 6lo and CoRE, that could benefit from the IETF IE. The 6TiSCH Working Group has already expressed the need for the IE, and this allocation is expected to satisfy that need.

The document is also explicit about how the element is allocated. Per the IETF's request, the IEEE 802.15 Working Group has allocated an ID, 5, for a Payload IE for IETF use, and the IETF understands that this is the only ID it will be issued.
sections.plainLanguage: Several IETF working groups have protocols that could ride in this element, and one of them had already asked for it. The IEEE working group gave the IETF element number 5, and that is the only number the IETF will get.

sections.title: The Subtype ID Registry
sections.content:
The registry of IEEE Std 802.15.4 IETF IE Subtype IDs has been created. Value 0 is Reserved, values 1 to 200 are Unassigned, and values 201 to 255 are for Experimental Use. Any change or addition to this registry requires Expert Review.

The document notes that vendor-specific IEs are already defined in IEEE 802.15.4, and that because of this there is no need to reserve any subtype IDs for vendor-specific uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers inside the element are allocated by IANA. The first 200 are free for real protocols, the last 55 are for experiments, and the first one is kept in reserve in case a wider field is ever needed. Changing the list needs expert review.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document creates an IANA registry for IETF IE subtype IDs, and the security of the protocols using the IEs MUST be described in the documents requesting allocations from this registry.

IEEE Std 802.15.4 contains methods in which the security of an IE can be enforced when a frame is received, but this is only per IE type. Therefore all IETF IEs have the same security-level requirements regardless of the subtype ID used. This can cause issues if different security processing would be needed and any of those IEs would need to be processed at the MAC level. Since all IETF protocols should operate at a higher level than the MAC level, the higher-layer processing for these IEs SHOULD perform separate security policy checking based on the IETF IE subtype ID in addition to the checks done by the MAC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol that uses the element has to describe its own security, because the standard only checks the element as a whole. The layer above should therefore apply its own policy per subtype, on top of the checks the radio layer already does.

items.title: Subtype ID
items.text: One octet, allocated by IANA. The value 0 is reserved in case a longer field is ever needed.

items.title: Subtype content
items.text: The actual content of the element; its length comes from the Length field of the IETF IE.

items.title: Maximum content length
items.text: The maximum length of the Payload IE content is 2047 octets.

items.title: Several per frame
items.text: One 802.15.4 frame may contain multiple IETF IEs with the same or different subtypes.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: Held for future extensibility, in case a longer subtype ID field is needed.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Available for subtypes allocated from the registry.

items.label: Experimental Use
items.desc: Set aside for experimental use of subtype IDs.
